title: Sudden pleuritic chest pain after a long-haul flight
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 51-year-old woman in a metropolitan ED with sudden, sharp chest pain that woke her, breathlessness and a swollen right leg. The candidate then interprets her observations, ECG, bloods and CT pulmonary angiogram, justifies the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism from her risk factors, and outlines management and safety netting.
focus: Acute pleuritic chest pain: eliciting VTE risk factors, excluding the red-flag differentials, and confirming and managing pulmonary embolism
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. It is late in the evening. Bertha Jones, a 51-year-old woman, has come in with chest pain. She is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken her observations, recorded an ECG and sent bloods.
tasks: Take a focused history from Bertha and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, ECG, blood results and CT pulmonary angiogram report. Interpret them and justify your diagnosis using her risk factors, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Bertha Jones, a 51-year-old retired accountant. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You were born in England and have lived in Australia for many years. You are frightened and in a lot of pain. You sit upright, take shallow breaths and wince when you breathe in deeply or cough. You can speak in sentences. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Bertha came in about 15 minutes ago. At triage her heart rate was 112 and regular, BP 132/84, resp rate 26, sats 93% on room air, temperature 37.6, pain 10 out of 10. The repeat a few minutes ago was RR 28, sats 92%, HR 116, BP 126/80. The ECG is done, the cannula is in and bloods have gone to the lab."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they ask the nurse to give oxygen, your sats come up to 96% and you feel a little less short of breath.
  • If they offer pain relief and the nurse gives it, the pain eases to about 5/10 over 10 minutes and you can take a slightly deeper breath.
  • If they explain calmly what they are doing, you settle a little. If they use jargon, ask them what it means.
  • If they ask for a scan or blood results now, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.

Opening line: "Doctor, my chest really hurts!"

History (give only when asked):

The chest pain

  • Site: the middle and right side of your chest, low down. It does not spread anywhere (only say this if asked about spread).
  • Character: sharp and stabbing.
  • Severity: 10/10. "It woke me from my sleep!"
  • Onset: sudden, about 1 hour ago.
  • Pattern: constant since then, neither better nor worse.
  • Worse with: breathing in, coughing and sneezing. Nothing makes it better. Leaning forward does not help.
  • Previous episodes: none. You have never had pain like this.

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Breathless since the pain started.
  • Palpitations: your heart is racing, but it feels regular.
  • Right leg: for 3 days your right calf has been painful, tender, red and swollen. You thought you had strained it walking around Heathrow airport.
  • No cough, no coughing up blood, no fever, sweats or shivers. No recent cold or flu and no sick contacts.
  • The pain is not crushing or heavy. It does not go to your neck, jaw, arms or back. No nausea or vomiting. No fainting or near-fainting.
  • No weight loss and no unusual tiredness before tonight.
  • No injury to your chest, no falls. The chest wall itself is not sore to touch.
  • No rash on your chest or back. You do not remember having chickenpox.
  • No tummy pain, indigestion or change in your bowels.
  • No history of anxiety or other mental health problems, though you are frightened now.

Clot risk (only if asked)

  • Travel: you flew back from the UK 4 days ago after visiting family. It was a long-haul flight of about 22 hours of flying, and you sat in your seat for most of it because your knees ache when you walk.
  • Hormones: you take hormone replacement therapy (Femoston), started when your menopause was diagnosed last year.
  • No previous clots in your legs or lungs. No cancer. No recent operations, hospital stays or plaster casts. Not overweight. No clotting or blood disorders in you or your family.

Past medical history

  • Menopause, diagnosed last year.
  • Osteoarthritis in both knees.
  • Osteoporosis.
  • No heart, lung or kidney problems. No high blood pressure, diabetes or high cholesterol that you know of. No cancer. No stomach ulcers, no bleeding problems and no stroke (only if asked).
  • No Marfan syndrome or other connective tissue disease in you or your family (only if asked).

Medications

  • Femoston 2/10, one tablet daily (oestradiol 2 mg every day, with dydrogesterone 10 mg added in the second half of each 28-day pack).
  • Paracetamol modified release 1.33 g twice a day for your knees. You took your evening dose at about 8 pm.
  • Naproxen 500 mg twice a day for your knees.
  • Pantoprazole 20 mg daily. Your GP said it protects your stomach from the naproxen.
  • Denosumab (Prolia) 60 mg injection every 6 months for your bones.
  • No over-the-counter medicines or supplements. No blood thinners.

Allergies: penicillin. You had anaphylaxis to it, with throat swelling and collapse, and needed adrenaline.

Family history: your mother has osteoporosis. Nothing else, and no blood or clotting problems in the family.

Social history

  • Retired accountant. You live with your husband and manage everything at home yourself, including shopping, cooking and driving.
  • Strong social network: you go to a book club every week.
  • Smoking: current smoker, 10 cigarettes a day for 20 years.
  • No alcohol and no recreational drugs.
  • A balanced, healthy diet. You are fairly inactive because the arthritis limits how far you can walk.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are scared you are having a heart attack, because the pain is so bad. You did not think your sore leg had anything to do with it. You want the pain to stop and you want to know what is going on. Your husband is in the waiting room.

If the candidate asks whether anything else has been worrying you, say: "Is this a heart attack? Am I going to die?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: anxious, distressed by pain, sitting upright. Shallow, rapid breathing, speaking in full sentences. Not cyanosed, not pale, not sweaty. Looks well nourished (68 kg, BMI about 25). Nicotine staining on the right fingers.
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Pulse: 112/min, regular, good volume. Radial pulses equal on both sides, no radio-femoral delay.
  • Blood pressure: right arm 132/84, left arm 130/82.
  • Hands and peripheries: warm, capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing.
  • JVP: not raised.
  • Heart: dual heart sounds, normal P2, no murmurs, no pericardial rub. No right ventricular heave.
  • Chest wall: not tender to palpation. No bruising or deformity. No rash on the chest or back.
  • Respiratory: trachea central. Expansion equal but shallow because of pain. Resonant on percussion throughout. Vesicular breath sounds with equal air entry, no crackles, no wheeze, no pleural rub.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. No pulsatile mass.
  • Legs: right calf swollen, red and warm, with pitting oedema to the mid-shin. Tender along the deep veins of the calf and in the popliteal fossa. Calf circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity is right 40 cm, left 36 cm (4 cm difference). Left leg normal. No varicose veins. Pedal pulses present on both sides. Bony crepitus in both knees, no effusion.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Bertha's identity and asks whether she is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Acknowledges her pain and fear, offers analgesia early and keeps questions short and focused because she is breathless and in pain.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site: central and right lower chest, no radiation
Character and severity: sharp, stabbing, 10/10, woke her from sleep
Time course: sudden onset 1 hour ago, constant, unchanged, no previous episodes
Pleuritic: worse with breathing in, coughing and sneezing

check.x: Asks about associated cardiorespiratory symptoms: breathlessness and palpitations (both present, palpitations regular), syncope and haemoptysis (absent).
Elicits the painful, red, swollen right calf for 3 days.

Asks about VTE risk factors: recent travel (long-haul flight from the UK 4 days ago), oestrogen (HRT), reduced mobility (knee osteoarthritis), smoking, recent surgery, cancer, previous DVT or PE, and family history of clotting disorders.
check.d: Credit when at least 4 risk factors are asked about, including the flight and the HRT.

check.x: Asks about features of the red-flag differentials:
check.d: Credit when ACS, aortic dissection and pneumothorax features are asked about, plus at least one of pericarditis or pneumonia.

kids.x: ACS: crushing or heavy pain, radiation to the arm, neck or jaw, nausea, sweating
Aortic dissection: tearing pain to the back, syncope, hypertension, connective tissue disease
Pneumothorax: chest trauma, lung disease such as COPD
Pericarditis: recent viral illness, pain eased by leaning forward
Pneumonia: cough, fever, sweats, sick contacts

check.x: Screens other systems: weight loss and fatigue (malignancy), GI symptoms, chest wall injury (musculoskeletal pain), rash (shingles), and anxiety.
Takes the past medical history: menopause last year, knee osteoarthritis, osteoporosis; no cardiac, respiratory, cancer or clotting history.

Takes a full medication history, including the oestrogen-containing HRT (Femoston), regular naproxen and modified-release paracetamol, and confirms she takes no anticoagulant. Asks about bleeding, ulcers and stroke before anticoagulation.
Asks about allergies and the reaction: penicillin anaphylaxis.
Takes a family history: mother has osteoporosis; no clotting or blood disorders.

Takes a social history: quantifies smoking (10 a day for 20 years, 10 pack-years), alcohol and drugs (none), and function (retired, lives with her husband, independent, sedentary because of her knees).
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: fears a heart attack and dying, did not link the leg to the chest pain, wants pain relief and answers.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: distress, work of breathing, speech in sentences, cyanosis, and the nurse's observations (HR 112, RR 26, SpO2 93% on room air).
Cardiovascular examination: pulse rate and rhythm, BP in both arms, peripheral perfusion, JVP, heart sounds including P2, murmurs, rub and RV heave.
Respiratory examination: trachea, expansion, percussion and auscultation for pneumothorax, consolidation, effusion or a pleural rub (all normal apart from shallow breathing).
Palpates the chest wall for tenderness (none) and inspects for a rash.
Examines both legs for DVT and finds the right calf swollen, red, warm and tender along the deep veins with pitting oedema, measuring calf circumference (4 cm larger on the right).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone and worsening between sets, needing clinical review and senior escalation. Tachycardic (white zone) with a normal BP, so not haemodynamically unstable.
Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia at 112/min with no ischaemic ST change and no S1Q3T3, RBBB or other sign of right heart strain.

Interprets the bloods: normal hs-troponin (no myocardial injury, against ACS and RV strain), normal renal function (safe for contrast and DOAC dosing), normal Hb, platelets and clotting as a baseline before anticoagulation.
Calculates Wells as 7.5 (clinical DVT 3, PE most likely 3, HR over 100 1.5), so PE is likely and a D-dimer is not indicated.
Interprets the CTPA as acute bilateral PE (predominantly right-sided) with a small right lower lobe infarct and no RV strain.

Gives the diagnosis as acute pulmonary embolism with a right leg DVT, provoked. Justifies it with at least two of: the history (sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness, 3 days of right calf swelling), the investigations (sinus tachycardia, CTPA) and the risk factors (long-haul flight, oestrogen HRT, limited mobility, smoking).

Risk stratifies: haemodynamically stable with no RV dysfunction and a normal troponin, so not high-risk PE. sPESI is 1 (HR 110 or more), so she is not suitable for outpatient treatment and is admitted.
Management
Escalates to the senior ED doctor or medical registrar and continues cardiac monitoring with regular observations.

Prescribes oxygen to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96% (TSANZ): starts low-flow oxygen if SpO2 falls below 92%, or now given the worsening trend. Gives analgesia: titrated IV opioid, with paracetamol kept within the daily maximum (she already takes modified-release paracetamol). No extra NSAID.

Starts anticoagulation promptly after checking bleeding risk, with a correct regimen: apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily with food, or enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily.
States that thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk PE with haemodynamic instability and is not indicated here, and that an IVC filter is only for patients who cannot be anticoagulated.
Stops naproxen (bleeding risk with anticoagulation) and stops the oestrogen HRT (a VTE risk factor). Plans to discuss menopause symptom alternatives with her GP.

Admits her under the medical team and plans at least 3 months of anticoagulation for provoked VTE, reviewed at 3 months. Thrombophilia testing is not routinely needed. Offers smoking cessation support (NRT in hospital, Quitline).

Explains in plain words that a blood clot from the leg has travelled to the lungs, that it is not a heart attack, and that blood thinners stop it growing while the body clears it. Checks understanding.
Safety netting

Tells Bertha in plain words to tell the nurse at once, or call 000 after discharge, for worsening breathlessness or chest pain, fainting, coughing up blood, or signs of bleeding (black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, vomiting blood, a severe headache, heavy bruising).
Arranges GP review within about a week of discharge and a 3-month review of the anticoagulant, and advises her not to stop it without medical advice.

part2.lead: Here are her observations, the ECG the nurse recorded, her blood results and the CT pulmonary angiogram report.
part2.patient:
Ask these only after the examiner reads question 4, one at a time:

  • "Was it the hormone tablets? Do I have to stop them? The hot flushes were awful before."
  • "Will I be on blood thinners forever?"

You are relieved it is not a heart attack. If the candidate explains clearly and kindly, you accept the plan and ask them to tell your husband. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets taken on room air before any treatment; the 22:10 set was taken just before you arrived.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 26 and SpO2 93% on room air are in the yellow zone. HR 112, BP 132/84 and temperature 37.6 °C are white, and the pain is severe (10/10). At 22:10 RR 28 and SpO2 92% are still yellow and slightly worse, HR has risen to 116 (white), and BP 126/80 is maintained.
  • Meaning: tachypnoea, hypoxia and tachycardia with sudden pleuritic pain fit PE. BP is normal, so there is no shock and no high-risk (massive) PE. A white-zone heart rate does not mean she is well, and the trend is worsening.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior review now. Oxygen to keep SpO2 92 to 96%, analgesia, and continued monitoring. A move into the red zone (SBP below 90, SpO2 in the red zone, HR 140 or more) calls for a rapid response and reassessment for high-risk PE.

rows.note: Triage: to acute bay, monitor on, ECG requested
Repeat set at bedside before medical review

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mrs Bertha Jones, age 51, recorded at 22:05 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 112/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +60°.
  • PR interval: 150 ms.
  • QRS duration: 88 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 430 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression in any lead. T waves upright in I, II, aVL, aVF and V1 to V6; T inversion in aVR only (normal).
  • Other: no S wave in I with Q wave and T inversion in III. No right axis deviation. No P pulmonale. No pathological Q waves. Normal R wave progression.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 112/min with a normal axis and normal intervals. No ST or T wave changes, no S1Q3T3, no RBBB, no right axis deviation and no anterior T inversion.
  • Meaning: sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. There are no signs of right heart strain and no ischaemic changes, which makes STEMI unlikely. A normal ECG apart from the tachycardia neither confirms nor excludes PE.
  • Changes: PE stays the working diagnosis and needs imaging. Repeat the ECG if the pain changes.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.result: Venous sample collected 22:05, about 1 hour after the pain began.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb, WCC, neutrophils and platelets are normal. Electrolytes, urea and creatinine are normal, with eGFR above 90. ALT and bilirubin are normal. INR and APTT are normal. hs-troponin I is 5 ng/L, below the women's 99th percentile of 16.
  • Meaning: there is no myocardial injury. That argues against ACS, though one early troponin does not exclude it alone, and points to no RV strain from the PE. There is no infection on the bloods.
  • Changes: renal function is safe for iodinated contrast and for full-dose DOAC or enoxaparin without adjustment. The normal blood count, liver tests and clotting are a baseline before anticoagulation.

handover.label: CT pulmonary angiogram
handover.result:
Examination: CT pulmonary angiogram, after IV iodinated contrast (pulmonary arterial phase), 23:05.

Clinical details: 51-year-old woman with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, 3 days of right calf swelling, a long-haul flight 4 days ago, on oestrogen HRT. HR 112, SpO2 93% on room air. High clinical suspicion of PE.

Findings:

  • Pulmonary arteries: good opacification. Filling defects in the right interlobar artery, extending into the right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental arteries. A non-occlusive filling defect in the left lower lobe posterobasal segmental artery. Main pulmonary artery 26 mm (normal calibre).
  • Right heart: RV to LV diameter ratio 0.8. No flattening or bowing of the interventricular septum. No reflux of contrast into the IVC or hepatic veins.
  • Lungs: a small wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity in the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe, in keeping with early pulmonary infarction. No consolidation elsewhere. No mass or suspicious nodule.
  • Pleura: trace right pleural effusion. No pneumothorax.
  • Mediastinum and heart: heart size normal. No pericardial effusion. No lymphadenopathy. Thoracic aorta of normal calibre with no intimal flap seen (non-gated pulmonary arterial phase study).
  • Bones and soft tissues: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: acute bilateral pulmonary emboli, predominantly right-sided, with a small right lower lobe pulmonary infarct. No CT evidence of right heart strain. No pneumothorax or consolidation.
handover.model:
• Read: filling defects in the right interlobar artery and the right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental arteries, plus a left lower lobe segmental embolus, so the emboli are bilateral. The RV to LV ratio is below 1 with no septal bowing or contrast reflux, so there is no RV strain. There is a small right lower lobe infarct with a trace effusion. No pneumothorax, no consolidation, and the aorta looks normal.
  • Meaning: this confirms acute PE. The pleural-based infarct explains the pleuritic pain and low-grade temperature. With the right calf signs, this is VTE provoked by the flight, oestrogen and immobility. Normal BP, no RV strain and a normal troponin make it intermediate-low risk (sPESI 1 from the heart rate).
  • Changes: start therapeutic anticoagulation now and admit under the medical team. Thrombolysis is not indicated. A leg ultrasound does not change management now that PE is confirmed.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Bertha Jones, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer using her risk factors and her pretest probability.
Outline your management of Bertha now, here in the emergency department.
Bertha has some questions about what caused this and her treatment. Please answer her, then tell me what warning signs you would teach her and what follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Bertha Jones, 51.
  • Situation: acute bilateral PE on CTPA. RR 28 and SpO2 92% on room air (yellow zone, worsening), HR 116, BP 126/80.
  • Background: sudden pleuritic central and right lower chest pain 1 hour, breathlessness, 3 days of right calf swelling; flight from the UK 4 days ago, oestrogen HRT, knee OA limiting mobility, smoker; on naproxen; penicillin anaphylaxis.
  • Assessment: ECG sinus tachycardia, no ischaemia or right heart strain; troponin normal; renal function and clotting normal; CTPA bilateral PE with a small RLL infarct, no RV strain. Wells 7.5; haemodynamically stable, sPESI 1, so intermediate-low risk.
  • Recommendation: starting anticoagulation; please review and admit under medicine.

Acute pulmonary embolism with a right DVT, provoked: Wells 7.5 (PE likely), so straight to CTPA, no D-dimer; sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness; 3 days of a swollen, tender right calf; long-haul flight, oestrogen HRT, limited mobility, smoking; sinus tachycardia; CTPA filling defects.

  • ACS: against: sharp pleuritic pain, no radiation, normal ECG and troponin.
  • Aortic dissection: against: no tearing or back pain, equal arm BPs, normal aorta on CT.
  • Pneumothorax: against: normal percussion and breath sounds, none on CT.
  • Pericarditis: against: no viral prodrome, not positional, no rub, normal ECG.
  • Pneumonia with pleurisy: against: no cough or fever, normal WCC, no consolidation.

1. Senior review; continuous monitoring; oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96%.
  2. Analgesia: titrated IV opioid; paracetamol within the 4 g daily maximum, counting her modified-release paracetamol; no extra NSAID.
  3. Anticoagulate now after checking bleeding risk: apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, or enoxaparin 1 mg/kg (about 70 mg) twice daily.
  4. No thrombolysis (stable, no RV strain); IVC filter only if anticoagulation is contraindicated.
  5. Stop naproxen and the oestrogen HRT; continue pantoprazole.
  6. Admit under medicine (sPESI 1); at least 3 months of anticoagulation for provoked VTE; no routine thrombophilia testing.
  7. Smoking cessation: NRT, Quitline.

• Cause: a clot formed in the leg after the long flight, made more likely by the hormone tablets, less walking and smoking, and travelled to the lungs. Not a heart attack.
  • HRT: stop it; her GP will discuss other options for hot flushes.
  • Duration: at least 3 months, reviewed then; do not stop without advice.
  • Red flags (000): worse breathlessness or chest pain, fainting, coughing blood; bleeding signs such as black stools, blood in the urine, vomiting blood, severe headache, heavy bruising.
  • Follow-up: GP within about 1 week; 3-month review (GP or thrombosis clinic); quit smoking support; review of arthritis pain relief.

ddx.dx: Acute pulmonary embolism with right leg deep vein thrombosis, provoked
ddx.for: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after 3 days of a swollen, tender right calf, a long-haul flight 4 days ago, oestrogen HRT, limited mobility and smoking, with sinus tachycardia and bilateral filling defects on CTPA.
She is a 51-year-old smoker with severe chest pain, tachycardia and fear of a heart attack.
ddx.against: The pain is sharp and pleuritic with no radiation, nausea or sweating, and the ECG and hs-troponin are normal.
No tearing pain or radiation to the back, no syncope or hypertension, equal arm BPs, and a normal-calibre aorta with no flap on CT.

ddx.for: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness in a smoker.
ddx.against: No chest trauma or lung disease, the trachea is central, percussion and breath sounds are normal, and CT shows no pneumothorax.

ddx.for: Sharp central chest pain worse on breathing in, with a low-grade temperature.
ddx.against: No preceding viral illness, the pain is not eased by leaning forward, there is no rub and the ECG shows no widespread ST elevation.

ddx.for: Pleuritic chest pain, tachypnoea, hypoxia and a temperature of 37.6 °C.
ddx.against: No cough, sputum, fever or sick contacts, normal chest examination and WCC, and no consolidation on CT apart from a small infarct.

guide:
In Part 1, Bertha answers the history and the nurse gives the opening observations. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Give the right calf findings only if the candidate examines the legs. If the candidate asks for a D-dimer, CTPA or results in Part 1, say these will be given in Part 2. Credit a candidate who says a D-dimer is not needed because the pretest probability is high. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Bertha asks her questions after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pleuritic pain, elicits the swollen right calf and every VTE risk factor (flight, HRT, immobility, smoking), and quickly excludes features of ACS, dissection, pneumothorax, pericarditis and pneumonia. They check bleeding risk and the penicillin anaphylaxis and examine both legs. In Part 2 they read the ECG as sinus tachycardia only, calculate Wells at 7.5, confirm bilateral PE without RV strain on CTPA, and justify the diagnosis with history, results and risk factors. They start a correctly dosed anticoagulant, stop naproxen and the oestrogen HRT, explain why thrombolysis is not indicated, admit her and safety-net in plain words.

A borderline candidate takes a generic chest pain history, misses the leg, the flight or the HRT, and does not examine the legs. They may call the ECG normal without naming sinus tachycardia, order a D-dimer in a high-probability patient, or forget to stop the naproxen and HRT. Discharging her without anticoagulation, or giving thrombolysis to a stable patient, is a serious safety concern.
explain:
Diagnosis: provoked pulmonary embolism with a right leg DVT

Bertha has an acute pulmonary embolism (PE) that came from a right calf deep vein thrombosis (DVT). PE is an important and preventable cause of illness and death, and it must be considered in every patient with chest pain or breathlessness. Her story is typical. She had sudden pleuritic chest pain that woke her, breathlessness and a racing heart, after 3 days of a painful, red, swollen right calf. She has several risk factors: a long-haul flight 4 days ago, oral oestrogen HRT, reduced mobility from knee osteoarthritis, and current smoking.

The history

  • Symptoms of PE: sudden breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, syncope and haemoptysis.
  • Signs: tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia, hypotension in massive PE, and signs of DVT. Homans' sign is a classic DVT sign but it is unreliable.
  • Risk factors: previous VTE; a personal or family history of clotting disorders; malignancy; oestrogen (HRT or the combined pill); pregnancy; obesity; surgery, especially orthopaedic; immobilisation (travel, injury, hospital stay); trauma; smoking; older age.
  • Ruling out the dangerous mimics: ACS (crushing pain radiating to the arm, neck or jaw, with nausea or sweating), aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back, syncope, hypertension, connective tissue disease), pneumothorax (trauma, COPD), pericarditis (a viral prodrome, pain eased by leaning forward) and pneumonia (cough, fever, sick contacts). Chest wall tenderness suggests costochondritis. Shingles pain can come before the rash.
  • Before anticoagulation: ask about bleeding, peptic ulcer, stroke, current antiplatelets, NSAIDs and anticoagulants, and allergies.

Pretest probability: Wells and PERC

Clinical suspicion of PE is followed by a formal pretest probability. In the two-level Wells score, clinical signs of DVT score 3, PE as the most likely diagnosis 3, HR above 100 1.5, immobilisation for at least 3 days or surgery in the previous 4 weeks 1.5, previous DVT or PE 1.5, haemoptysis 1 and malignancy 1. A score above 4 means PE is likely. Bertha scores 7.5. In the NSW ACI PE evaluation pathway, a patient in the PE-likely group goes straight to imaging. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: a negative result helps rule out PE only when the pretest probability is not high. It also rises in pregnancy, trauma, recent surgery, heart disease, infection and older age.

PERC (the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria) is used only when the pretest probability is low. If all 8 criteria are negative, no further testing for PE is needed. Bertha is not low probability, and she fails PERC anyway on age (51), heart rate, SpO2, oestrogen use and unilateral leg swelling.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 are in the yellow zone and worsening, which calls for a clinical review. Her BP is normal, so this is not high-risk (massive) PE.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. Other findings include S1Q3T3 and signs of right heart strain: RBBB, right axis deviation, and T inversion in V1 to V4, with or without II, III and aVF. A normal ECG does not exclude PE.
  • Bloods: a normal troponin argues against myocardial injury from ACS or RV strain. Normal renal and liver function and a normal blood count and clotting allow contrast imaging and standard anticoagulant doses.
  • CTPA: bilateral emboli with a small right lower lobe infarct, which explains the pleuritic pain in her right lower chest, and no RV strain. If CTPA is contraindicated, a V/Q scan is the alternative. Compression ultrasound of the legs confirms a DVT when the leg is clinically suggestive, but it does not change treatment once PE is confirmed.

Risk stratification

Severity is graded by haemodynamic status, RV function and troponin. High-risk PE has haemodynamic instability (shock or sustained hypotension). Bertha is stable, with no RV dysfunction on CT and a normal troponin. Her sPESI is 1 (HR 110 or more), so she is not low risk and not suitable for outpatient treatment. She is admitted.

Management

  1. Supportive care: monitoring, oxygen titrated to SpO2 92 to 96% (TSANZ), and analgesia with titrated opioid. Her daily paracetamol must stay within the maximum because she already takes modified-release paracetamol. No extra NSAID.
  2. Anticoagulation (eTG, THANZ) starts as soon as PE is confirmed, or before imaging if suspicion is high and imaging is delayed, once bleeding risk has been checked. Options include apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily; rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg once daily with food; or enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily followed by an oral agent. Warfarin needs LMWH overlap until the INR is therapeutic.
  3. Duration: THANZ recommends at least 3 months for all VTE. After 3 months, provoked VTE with a transient risk factor that has been removed can usually stop; extended therapy is considered after unprovoked VTE.
  4. Risk factor optimisation: stop naproxen, which adds bleeding risk with an anticoagulant. Stop the oral oestrogen HRT, and plan menopause symptom management with her GP. Offer smoking cessation (NRT in hospital, Quitline) and review her arthritis pain relief.
  5. Case by case: thrombolysis only for high-risk (massive) PE with haemodynamic instability, where the benefit outweighs the bleeding risk. An IVC filter only when anticoagulation is contraindicated. Thrombophilia testing only for recurrent or atypical VTE, not routinely after provoked VTE.

Safety netting and follow-up

Bertha needs to know to seek help at once (000) for worsening breathlessness or chest pain, fainting or coughing up blood, and for signs of bleeding on anticoagulation: black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, vomiting blood, a severe headache or heavy bruising. She should not stop the anticoagulant without advice. Follow-up is a GP review within about a week of discharge and a review at 3 months (GP, haematology or thrombosis clinic) to decide the duration of anticoagulation. Her HRT, arthritis pain relief and smoking also need ongoing review, along with advice about mobility and hydration on future long flights.
points: Ask every patient with pleuritic chest pain or breathlessness about VTE risk factors (travel, oestrogen, immobility, surgery, cancer, previous VTE, smoking), and examine both legs.
Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. S1Q3T3 and right heart strain are less common, and a normal ECG does not exclude PE.
Use Wells to set pretest probability: above 4 means PE is likely, so go straight to CTPA. D-dimer rules out PE only when probability is not high, and PERC applies only to low-probability patients.
Grade severity by haemodynamics, RV strain and troponin. Thrombolysis is only for high-risk PE with instability; sPESI 1 or more means admission rather than outpatient care.
Start a correctly dosed anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban or enoxaparin) once bleeding risk is checked, for at least 3 months, and stop NSAIDs and oestrogen therapy.
Safety-net in plain words: symptoms of a new or bigger clot and signs of bleeding on anticoagulation both need 000, plus GP follow-up and a 3-month review of the anticoagulant.
